summary: CELESTIAL CHARM — Mars Mission: Outpost Operations is an interactive, bilingual (English/Spanish) web-based STEM simulator inspired by NASA’s Mars exploration programs. Designed for students and young learners, it places users in the role of Junior Mission Control flight directors managing Habitat Alpha (Sector 04, Jezero Crater). Across six missions that can be played in any order, each with three decisions (18 in total), players respond to a coronal mass ejection, guide an autonomous rover, evaluate Martian terrain, shield the crew from radiation, counter spaceflight bone-density loss, and verify a radio-astronomy signal. Every choice consumes energy and changes six reserves: Oxygen, Water, Energy, Food, Materials, and Shielding. Players can also spend Materials on five surface upgrades. Their progress appears in a pixel-art outpost map and an animated astronaut helmet view. Each mission includes a sourced scientific brief, and a Solar System Atlas with all eight planets and links to NASA, CSA, and SETI resources lets learners continue exploring real planetary data.
details:
Executive Summary

CELESTIAL CHARM is an interactive STEM simulation platform inspired by NASA’s planetary science, space weather, and human spaceflight research. Traditional space education often relies on passive reading, leaving students disconnected from the engineering constraints and life-support trade-offs that astronauts and flight controllers face on another world. CELESTIAL CHARM bridges this gap by placing learners in a simulated telemetry and decision-making environment set at Habitat Alpha, Sector 04, in Jezero Crater, Mars (18.4° N, 77.5° E).

Through six scenario-driven missions—each structured into three sequential decisions—students manage six interdependent outpost resources, build surface upgrades, follow an animated first-person astronaut helmet view (Live POV), and explore a Solar System Atlas and a hub of open-science resources (NASA DONKI, NASA OSDR, NASA Mars Trek, and the Canadian Space Agency, with SETI Institute material linked in Mission 06 and the final report).

You can see our Repository in Github: https://github.com/celestianchram/celestian-chram

1. Project Description

1.1. What Does It Do?

CELESTIAL CHARM simulates surface operations at a Martian research outpost (ARTEMIS · MARS-06) under illustrative extreme conditions, shown in the Surface View panel as a temperature of −63 °C and 43% solar light. Specifically, the platform enables users to:

  • Command six Mars missions: Select and complete six distinct operations: coronal mass ejection (CME) alert and shelter, autonomous rover routing to the delta, dust-front landing-site selection, radiation sheltering, microgravity bone-health countermeasures, and radio-astronomy signal verification (the Wow! signal).
  • Manage six crew reserves: Monitor live meters and numerical counters (0 to 20 scale) for Oxygen (O₂), Water, Energy, Food, Materials, and Shielding. Oxygen, Water, Food, and Energy show a low-reserve warning at 3 units or fewer, and an overall status indicator reads SYSTEMS NOMINAL, MONITOR RESERVES, or CRITICAL RESERVES according to the lowest of those four.
  • Build surface upgrades: Spend Materials in the Build and Upgrade (Surface Engineering) panel on five one-time modules: Greenhouse, Water Recycler, Solar Panel, Science Lab, and Protective Dome.
  • Watch the outpost grow and see through the astronaut’s eyes: Follow progress in a side-panel pixel-art Live Construction map and in a first-person helmet visor (Live POV) with animated target markers, suit readouts, and phase-specific surface hardware.
  • Explore planetary science and open data: Open an interactive Solar System Atlas with all eight planets and follow links to free resources from NASA, the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), and the SETI Institute.
  • Switch language instantly: Use the English/Spanish toggle at any time.

1.2. How Does It Work?

The simulator runs on a state-and-resource loop organized into six steps:

  1. Initialization and free mission selection: Habitat Alpha begins with baseline reserves of 8 Oxygen, 8 Water, 7 Energy, 8 Food, 10 Materials, 2 Shielding, and 0 Science Points. Players select any of the six missions from the Mission Track, in any order.
  2. Three-decision structure: Each mission has three consecutive decisions (18 decisions and 54 options across a full campaign). In each one, players read an operational situation, review a Mission Brief with a sourced scientific fact (on the first decision of each mission), and choose action A, B, or C.
  3. Energy cost and resource trade-offs: Every confirmed decision consumes 1 unit of Energy, and the chosen option also changes specific reserves or adds Science Points.
  4. Surface engineering upgrades: At any point before the campaign ends, players can spend Materials (4 or 5 units per module) on a one-time upgrade that immediately boosts a reserve or adds points and appears on the pixel-art outpost map.
  5. End-of-mission life-support audit: When the third decision of a mission is completed, the crew consumes 1 Oxygen, 1 Water, and 1 Food. The campaign ends in failure, with a summary of the cause, if Energy is 0, if Oxygen, Water, or Food is 0, or if Shielding is 0 at the end of the radiation mission (Mission 04).
  6. Campaign completion and final score: Surviving all six missions gives a final score equal to the accumulated Science Points plus the sum of all remaining reserves, and opens a final report with a fact about the 1977 Wow! signal.

1.3. Innovation and Purpose

Core innovation: Unlike static quizzes or purely arcade space games, CELESTIAL CHARM couples quantitative resource budgeting with NASA-inspired mission scenarios and sourced scientific facts. Two visual panels—the pixel-art construction map and the astronaut helmet view—turn numerical decisions into immediate visual feedback, and the instant English/Spanish switch helps reduce language barriers in classrooms.

Purpose: To turn passive reading about astronomy into active problem-solving, helping young learners understand why energy conservation, radiation shielding, autonomous robotics, and human physiology matter for a human mission to Mars.

1.4. Benefits and Impact

A. Social, Environmental, and Technological Benefits

  • Social: Offers free, bilingual (EN/ES) STEM learning, practices critical thinking under constraints, and can be used in classrooms as a team mission-control activity.
  • Environmental: Includes Water Recycler, Greenhouse, and Solar Panel modules that introduce learners to recycling water, growing food, and generating power as ways to manage scarce resources in an extreme environment.
  • Technological: Introduces learners to telemetry-style dashboards, autonomous rover navigation under communication delay, space-weather alerts, and browser-based scientific simulation.

B. Contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Space Missions

  • SDG 4 – Quality Education: Delivers a free, browser-based, interactive learning experience linked to open educational and scientific resources.
  • SDG 9 – Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure: Encourages interest in aerospace engineering, robotics, solar energy, and resilient habitat infrastructure.
  • Alignment with space missions: Reflects themes of NASA’s Moon to Mars and Artemis exploration by simulating surface habitat operations, space-weather protection, and human–robotic cooperation.

C. Expected Community Impact

CELESTIAL CHARM gives educators, science clubs, and students a zero-cost digital activity that sparks curiosity in astronomy, planetary geology, and space biology while practicing evidence-based decision-making.

1.5. Objectives and Expected Results

Main objective: To design, develop, and deploy an interactive, bilingual educational web simulator that teaches young learners about the scientific, technological, and physiological challenges of operating a human outpost on Mars.

  • Spark student interest in astronomy and space exploration.
  • Teach quantitative management of interdependent resources (O₂, water, food, energy, materials, and shielding).
  • Develop critical thinking, risk evaluation, and decision-making across multi-step scenarios.
  • Connect gameplay to open resources from NASA, CSA, and SETI.
  • Provide a responsive web design and seamless English/Spanish localization.

Expected results: A functional, cloud-hosted web application with six three-decision Mars missions, a five-module surface engineering shop, live simulated telemetry, two procedural graphic visualizers, an eight-planet Solar System Atlas, and an open-science resource section.

1.6. Methodology and Work Plan

The project followed an iterative educational-engineering methodology in six stages.

Project Phases and Timeline

Main Activities by Stage

  • Synthesize official scientific findings into concise briefs for middle- and high-school learners.
  • Structure a non-linear mission selector so learners can address surface emergencies in any order.
  • Program procedural SVG graphics for both the pixel-art construction map and the astronaut helmet view.
  • Integrate profiles for all eight planets with links to NASA planetary fact pages (and to Mars Trek for Mars).
  • Playtest all 18 decisions for resource balance, clarity, and bilingual text.

Intermediate Deliverables

  • Scientific reference notes (Mars surface baseline, May 2024 RAD solar storm measurement, microgravity bone loss, and Wow! signal history).
  • Decision tables mapping all 54 options to resource changes and science points.
  • Procedural SVG graphics for 6 outpost construction milestones, 5 engineering upgrades, and 18 astronaut POV scenes.
  • Responsive interface with layouts for desktop, tablet, and mobile screens, ARIA labels, and live regions.
  • Production deployment on Vercel.

Scientific Data, Simulation Parameters, and Observations

The simulator combines illustrative game values with empirical measurements cited in the Mission Brief of each mission. Resource changes for each option (for example, +2 shielding) are game-balance values designed for learning, not NASA measurements.1.7. Methodology and Tools

1.7.1. Tools and Software Used

  • Code editor and browser developer tools: Used for writing and debugging the code and testing mobile screen sizes.
  • Vercel: Cloud platform used for deployment and HTTPS web hosting.
  • Open-science portals (NASA, CSA, and SETI): Scientific references linked in the simulator: NASA DONKI, NASA Mars Trek, NASA OSDR, NASA Science, NASA Space Place, CSA STEM resources and Food Lab toolkit, and the SETI Institute’s Wow! signal page.

1.7.2. Programming Languages and Framework

The simulator is a single, self-contained web page that uses no external JavaScript frameworks, which keeps it fast and portable across devices:

  • HTML5: Semantic landmarks (header, main, aside, nav, section, article), ARIA labels, ARIA live regions (aria-live="polite") for messages and the mission log, and a modal dialog (role="dialog", aria-modal="true") for the Solar System Atlas.
  • CSS3: Design tokens as custom properties (--navy, --orange, --cream, --teal, --green, --red), CSS Grid layouts with responsive breakpoints at 850 px and 620 px, keyframe animations (visorScan, pixelPop, pulse, moonfloat, drive), and support for prefers-reduced-motion.
  • Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+): Wrapped in a strict-mode IIFE; manages mission state, resource calculations, the engineering upgrade shop, the mission activity log, keyboard shortcuts (Escape closes the atlas; Enter advances after a decision), and English/Spanish text switching through data-es and data-en attributes.
  • Procedural SVG graphics: Generated in code for the pixel-art outpost map (viewBox 0 0 240 160, crisp edges) and the first-person astronaut helmet view (viewBox 0 0 900 290).

1.7.3. Hardware and Sensors

  • Hardware: A desktop computer, laptop, tablet, or smartphone with an internet connection to load the application and open external NASA, CSA, and SETI links, plus a monitor or projector for classroom demonstrations.
  • Sensors: The project does not use physical sensors. All environmental and crew values (temperature, sunlight, radiation alerts, oxygen, and energy) are simulated in software.

1.8. Project Management

Team Roles and Responsibilities Matrix


1.9. Project Location and Setting

Digital location: Cloud-hosted web application: https://celestian-chram.vercel.app/

Simulated location: Habitat Alpha, Sector 04 — Jezero Crater, Mars (18.4° N, 77.5° E).

Project justification: Jezero Crater is the exploration site of NASA’s Perseverance rover and preserves an ancient river delta of high geological and astrobiological interest. Setting the simulation there lets students look up the same region on NASA Mars Trek, which offers real image mosaics and elevation models.

1.10. Impact and Benefits (Relevance to NASA Missions and Strategic Goals)

CELESTIAL CHARM turns real planetary exploration challenges from NASA missions into six interactive operations:

  • Space weather and crew sheltering (Mission 01 — Coronal Mass Ejection Alert): Connects to NASA’s DONKI space-weather database and shows how a shelter sealed with regolith can reduce exposure to energetic solar particles.
  • Autonomous planetary robotics (Mission 02 — Mars Robot: Route to the Delta): Draws on Perseverance rover operations and shows why communication delay means a rover cannot be driven in real time.
  • Planetary cartography and site selection (Mission 03 — Dust Front and Landing-Site Selection): Applies Mars Trek concepts (terrain relief, slope, elevation models, sunlight, and nearby resources) to choose a safe outpost site.
  • Radiation dosimetry (Mission 04 — Radiation: Shelter the Crew): Uses the Curiosity RAD measurement from May 2024 (8,100 µGy) to teach limiting extravehicular activity (EVA), crew dosimetry, and shielding with regolith or water.
  • Space biology and crew health (Mission 05 — BioLab: Bones and Microgravity): Links to open NASA OSDR data and to microgravity bone loss (1%–1.5% per month without effective countermeasures), with options for ARED-style resistive exercise, nutrition, and crop growth.
  • Radio astronomy and scientific rigor (Mission 06 — WOW! Signal: Listen and Document): Uses the 1977 Big Ear detection to teach control-channel comparison, preserving original data and metadata, and reporting results without overstating the evidence.

1.11. Expected Results

  • A classroom-friendly web simulator with 6 missions, 18 decisions, and 54 options.
  • Improved student understanding of scarce-resource trade-offs and Martian environmental conditions.
  • Greater student engagement with NASA, CSA, and SETI open resources through mission links and the Solar System Atlas.
  • Easy adoption in English- and Spanish-speaking classrooms without specialized hardware.

1.12. Conclusions and Future Improvements

Conclusions

CELESTIAL CHARM shows that an interactive simulation can make aerospace engineering and planetary science concepts more engaging and accessible. By putting students in command of Habitat Alpha at Jezero Crater and challenging them to balance oxygen, water, food, energy, materials, and radiation shielding across NASA-inspired scenarios, the project supports the idea that scientific learning begins with a question and an evidence-based decision.

Lessons Learned

  • Systems interdependence: Operating an outpost requires balancing immediate crew survival (energy and life-support reserves) against scientific output and structural protection.
  • Scientific precision in educational tools: Grounding mission briefs in sourced measurements (such as Curiosity RAD radiation doses and NASA bone-loss estimates) and stating clearly that the Wow! signal is unconfirmed helps prevent misconceptions.
  • Accessible web architecture: Building with plain HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript keeps load times short and the application easy to run on classroom devices.

Possible Future Improvements

  • Live NASA API integration: Connect to the public NASA DONKI API to trigger mission alerts based on recent real-world solar storms.
  • Collaborative multiplayer mode: Allow student teams to take specialized flight-controller roles (Life Support, Rover Navigation, Space Weather, and BioLab).
  • Additional planetary campaigns: Expand to lunar south-pole operations (Artemis Base Camp) and icy moons such as Europa or Enceladus.
  • Educator data export: Let students download their decision log and resource history in PDF or CSV format for classroom grading.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

During the development of CELESTIAL CHARM, Artificial Intelligence tools were used responsibly as technical and editorial assistants under human supervision and scientific verification:

  • Information synthesis and bilingual drafting: Assisted in structuring technical documentation, organizing the six mission scenarios, and refining English and Spanish educational phrasing.
  • Code structuring assistance: Assisted in organizing JavaScript state logic, SVG graphic coordinates, and responsive CSS rules.
  • Scientific verification protocol: Scientific facts, measurements, and historical references shown in the simulator were checked against primary sources from NASA Science, NASA Mars Trek, NASA CCMC DONKI, NASA OSDR, the Canadian Space Agency, and the SETI Institute.
